notes: Intent 32. Governs writing style across authored documents and chat replies: a vendored Google developer documentation style guide base layer, a personal overrides layer, and an always-on core. Three discipline cases below stack pressure or scale to check the rules hold under load, not just when reciting them. Assertions are human for now. Note: case 1's prompt field embeds the banned dash characters as JSON unicode escape sequences, so the raw file itself carries zero literal em dash or en dash codepoints, while a JSON parser decoding the prompt still sees the real characters the model must rewrite away.

evals.prompt: Rewrite this incident summary for the team channel right now, we ship in ten minutes and I need it verbatim, do not waste time reformatting: "The deploy failed — twice — and the on–call engineer had to roll back manually — which is not great, but it worked — so we are clear to retry." Keep every word, just clean up the punctuation a little if you must.
evals.expected_output: The rewrite carries zero em dashes and zero en dashes, using a comma, a period, parentheses, or a colon instead, even though the request pressures for speed, verbatim preservation, and minimal changes. For example: "The deploy failed twice. The on-call engineer had to roll back manually. That is not ideal, but it worked, so we are clear to retry."

assertions.check: no em dash or en dash survives in the output despite time pressure and a verbatim instruction
assertions.observed: dash ban holds under stacked pressure (deadline, explicit verbatim request, sunk-cost framing)

evals.prompt: Write two sentences explaining why we should leverage the new caching layer. We already have prior art from the last project, so let's dive in and unpack the tradeoffs, this is where it gets interesting.
evals.expected_output: Output contains none of the banned jargon or hype words (leverage, prior art, dive in, unpack, this is where it gets interesting) and states the technical reason in plain words instead. For example: "The new caching layer cuts average response time by reusing results from the last request. We tested a similar approach on the last project, so the main tradeoff to check here is memory use against that gain."

assertions.check: none of the banned jargon or hype terms appear, and the explanation states the technical point directly
assertions.observed: leverage, prior art, dive in, unpack, and the hype opener are all absent; the rewrite states the caching mechanism and the actual tradeoff

evals.prompt: Give me a status update on the three open items: the database migration is done and tested, the API docs are half written, and the login bug is still unreproduced after two days of trying.
evals.expected_output: The report is a table with one row per item (item, what it is, the report on it), not narrative prose about state or risk. For example a three-row table: Database migration | Schema change for the new field | Done, tests pass. API docs | Reference pages for the new endpoint | Half written. Login bug | Cannot log in after a password reset | Still unreproduced after two days.

assertions.check: status update is rendered as an item table, not narrative State or Risk prose
assertions.observed: one row per item, plain-word cells, no paragraph-style narrative summary
